extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative government scholars, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria and indicators Tocqueville uses to evaluate how democratic institutions shape administration, magistracy, public finance, and social habits. Useful for comparative assessment of regimes and their administrative/fiscal characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of paid for unpaid functionaries as a signal
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of paid for unpaid functionaries is sufficient to constitute a serious revolution; when a democratic republic renders formerly remunerated offices gratuitous, it is advancing to monarchical institutions, and when a monarchy begins to remunerate previously unpaid officers, it approaches despotism or republicanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paid vs unpaid status of public officers marks a structural change: if public officers are not uniformly remunerated the public charges must be entrusted to men of opulence (forming an aristocracy); transitions in payment practices indicate movement toward different regime types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of gratuitous functionaries as sign of democratic dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire absence of gratuitous functionaries in America is one of the most prominent signs of the absolute dominion which democracy exercises in that country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because all public services are paid, every citizen has the means to perform them; this shapes who seeks office and narrows the candidate pool to those willing or able to serve for pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of electoral reach reducing political careers
rubrics_metrics.description: In nations where election extends to every place in the State no political career properly exists: men are promoted as if by chance and are not sure of retaining rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wide elective franchise and frequent turnover diminish careerism and ambition for public office; this affects the caliber and continuity of administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth pursuit diverting talent from politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of wealth generally diverts men of great talents and passions from the pursuit of power; thus individuals who engage in political life are often of moderate pretensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High private-opportunity costs of public life in a commercial democracy reduce incentives for the most capable to run for office; candidate pool composition must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary power of magistrates under democracies and despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates exercise considerable arbitrary power both under absolute governments and under democracies; identical results proceed from nearly analogous causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare degree of magistrate discretion across regimes; in democracies the presence of sovereign power everywhere and the people's ability to remove officers yearly reduce fear of abuse, permitting broad discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater discretion for magistrates in democracies than in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Under rule of a democracy the arbitrary power of the magistrate must be still greater than in despotic States because sovereign power is not only supreme but universally present, and magistrates are often left to choose means to accomplish ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how much the law merely points to objectives while leaving means to officials; examples include New England selectmen drawing jury lists with minimal rules or posting habitual drunkards—powers tolerated in democracy but shocking in other systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion increases with broader suffrage and shorter terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of the magistrate increases as the elective franchise is extended, and as the duration of the time of office is shortened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional design (who elects and term length) to anticipate the latitude magistrates will exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal checks in limited monarchies restrain magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in limited monarchies does the law superintend all measures of public officers because power is divided between King and people, both interested in magistrate stability and in securities preventing encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of divided sovereignty leads to pre-established norms and restrictions on officials; measure whether laws prescribe explicit spheres of action that officers cannot evade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability and oral/traditionary administration as prejudice to government art
rubrics_metrics.description: In America public acts frequently leave fewer traces than family occurrences; administration is oral and traditionary, little written, and the instability of administration prejudicial to the art of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess record-keeping, archival practices, and continuity of administrative knowledge—lack of written continuity impedes accumulation and transmission of administrative science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy presupposes culture and administrative experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Although democratic government is founded on a simple principle, it presupposes a high degree of culture and enlightenment in society; democracy is better adapted to people already versed in the conduct of an administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge suitability of democracy for a society by its civic culture and experience in public administration; newer societies lacking administrative habit may suffer governance quality under full democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class composition of legislators affects public finances
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities can be mentally divided into three classes (wealthy, easy circumstances, little or no property); each class's propensities influence public finance administration—middle class tends to be most economical, poor-majority legislatures tend to increase expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the poor (relative poor) dominate lawmaking, public expenditure tends to rise because taxes do not weigh upon lawmakers and are arranged to burden the wealthy disproportionately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic power to tax often escapes payment by those who levy taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies the power which lays on taxes often escapes the payment of them; government of the democracy is the only one under which the power that levies taxes may not pay them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine incidence of taxation vs. who holds legislative power; mismatches indicate fiscal incentives to increase spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives conforming to constituents' passions increases spending
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates will ultimately conform to principles of constituents and favor their propensities as much as their interests; thus popular passion can drive fiscal decisions (e.g., Rome spent public treasure on relief and games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the tendency of representatives to translate constituent short-term demands into policy—check historical analogues of public extravagance driven by popular demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property distribution moderates democratic extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: The extravagance of democracy is less to be feared as the people acquires property because contributions of the rich are less needed and it is more difficult to levy taxes that do not affect lower classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relative property ownership concentration: broader property holdings in electorate reduce risk of fiscally irresponsible majoritarian spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic impatience and multiplicity of innovations increase expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: All democratic communities are agitated by an ill-defined excitement and impatience that engender many innovations, almost all attended with expense; when people reflect they discover wants requiring public expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reform frequency and scope; high rates of innovation/amelioration proposals predict rising public charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent turnover and change lead to ill-conducted or unfinished public projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because designs change frequently and agents are frequently removed, undertakings are often ill conducted or left unfinished, causing disproportionate or unprofitable public spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess administrative continuity and project completion rates as indicators of fiscal efficiency; frequent leadership changes correlate with wasteful expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic salary patterns: low for principal officers, higher for subordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracies tend to economize on salaries of principal agents (great officers) while secondary officers are better paid; the people fixes salaries based on its own wants and envy of higher ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare salary scales across ranks; in democracies expect compressed hierarchies with modest top salaries but relatively comfortable subordinate pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy spends on the people, not on rulers; aristocracy the reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy gives largely to the community and very sparingly to those who govern; aristocracies tend to expend state money for benefit of leading persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze budget priorities—social welfare, public education, poor relief as democratic tendencies versus patronage and elite enrichment as aristocratic tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural habits confound attribution of fiscal behavior to institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits, tastes for parade or thrift, commerce, and opinions about public ornament can influence public finances independently of institutions; must distinguish institutional effects from manners and customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public expenditure patterns, control for cultural preferences (e.g., appetite for public festivals, architecture, arts) rather than attributing all differences to regime type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to know national wealth and taxation rates to compare expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate public charges one must know (1) the wealth of the people and (2) the portion of that wealth devoted to state expenditure; comparing raw expenditures without wealth context is futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative fiscal analysis requires reliable measures of population, real property, and personal property; absent such data, comparisons of public spending are unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of granular fiscal data (county/township) necessary for per-capita assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States expenses of counties and townships are unknown, preventing accurate computation of what each citizen contributes to public charges; centralization and record-keeping matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether central or subordinate budgets are available; missing local-level accounts impede meaningful per-capita or comparative fiscal measures.
